questions.subtopic: Joule–Thomson Cooling, Entropy and Work Properties
questions.question:
Which combination of the following statements is correct?
P. A gas cools upon expansion only when its Joule-Thomson coefficient is positive in the temperature range of expansion.
Q. For a system undergoing a process, its entropy remains constant only when the process is reversible.
R. the work done by a closed system in an adiabatic process is a point function.
S. A liquid expands upon freezing when the slope of its fusion curve on Pressure Temperature diagram is negative.
questions.explanation: Q is false: a closed system obeys ΔS = ∫δQ/T_boundary + S_gen. An irreversible nonadiabatic process can have ΔS = 0 if entropy carried out by heat transfer equals the positive entropy generated inside; entropy generation itself is never negative. P applies specifically to isenthalpic Joule–Thomson expansion: dT = μ_JT dp, so a pressure decrease cools the fluid where μ_JT > 0. Other expansion processes, including ideal-gas adiabatic expansion, can cool even though an ideal gas has μ_JT = 0. R also requires care: for a closed adiabatic system with negligible kinetic/potential changes, W = U₁ − U₂, so the work between specified endpoints within that constrained class is fixed. This does not turn work into a point/state property; work remains a transfer associated with a process. S is correct from dp/dT = h_fus/[T(v_liquid − v_solid)]: a negative fusion slope implies v_solid > v_liquid, so freezing expands the material. The printed a relies on calling constrained adiabatic work a point function and leaves P's throttling qualification unstated. Under a strict property definition no offered combination gives the defensible set, so the item is ungraded.

questions.subtopic: State Postulate for a Simple Compressible Substance
questions.question: The state of a simple compressible pure substance can be fixed by specifying
questions.explanation: The state postulate for a simple compressible pure substance in equilibrium requires two independent intensive properties, so b is correct. Once such a pair is fixed, the remaining thermodynamic properties follow. Temperature and specific volume are a useful independent pair in the usual single- and liquid–vapour two-phase regions considered here. Independence matters: during liquid–vapour equilibrium the saturation pressure fixes the saturation temperature, so p and T are not two independent specifications. This is why the source calls the postulate the two-property rule and explicitly requires independent intensive properties for a given mass.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.subtopic: Specific Volume after Removing a Steam Partition
questions.question: A vessel has two compartments. First compartment contains 2 kg of dry saturated steam at 7 bar [v_g at 7 bar = 0.27 m³/kg] and second compartment contains 1 kg of steam of dryness fraction of 0.8 at 3.5 bar [v_g at 3.5 bar = 0.55 m³/kg]. After the partition is removed, the pressure of the mixture is found to be 5 bar [v_g at 5 bar = 0.37 m³/kg]. Neglecting the volume of water, what will be specific volume of mixture?
questions.explanation: The total mass is m = m₁ + m₂ = 2 + 1 = 3 kg. Neglecting the liquid volume, the compartment specific volumes are x₁v_g1 = 1 × 0.27 and x₂v_g2 = 0.8 × 0.55 m³/kg. Thus the total vessel volume is V = 2(1 × 0.27) + 1(0.8 × 0.55) = 0.54 + 0.44 = 0.98 m³. Removing the partition changes neither the vessel volume nor the total mass, so the final mixture specific volume is v_m = V/m = 0.98/3 = 0.3267 m³/kg. Choice b, 0.326 m³/kg, is the intended and nearest offered value, with its final digits truncated. The stated final 5 bar value v_g = 0.37 m³/kg is not needed to find V/m; it would give x_m ≈ 0.3267/0.37 ≈ 0.883 under the same negligible-liquid-volume approximation.

questions.subtopic: Molar Mass of an Oxygen–Nitrogen Mixture
questions.question: The pressure and temperature of mixture of 4 kg O₂ and 6 kg N₂ are 4 bar and 27°C. What will be the value of molecular weight of mixture?
questions.explanation: The mixture molar mass is total mass divided by total amount of substance. With M_O₂ = 32 kg/kmol and M_N₂ = 28 kg/kmol, n_O₂ = 4/32 = 0.125 kmol and n_N₂ = 6/28 = 0.2142857 kmol. Hence M_mix = (4 + 6)/(4/32 + 6/28) = 10/0.3392857 = 29.4737 kg/kmol, which gives c, 29.47. Equivalently, 1/M_mix = w_O₂/M_O₂ + w_N₂/M_N₂. The pressure and temperature do not affect this composition calculation. The printed explanation wrongly averages molar masses using mass fractions: [(4 × 32) + (6 × 28)]/10 = 29.6. Arithmetic averaging of component molar masses requires mole fractions, not mass fractions.

questions.question: According to the state postulate, the number of independent properties required to determine the state of a system containing a pure substance, with two of its phases in equilibrium, is
questions.explanation: The state postulate requires two independent intensive properties to fix the complete state of a simple compressible system, giving b. For a liquid–vapour mixture one suitable pair is pressure and vapour quality x, or temperature and x. Saturation makes pressure and temperature dependent, so those two alone do not specify the amount of each phase and hence do not fix mixture-specific volume, enthalpy or entropy. Gibbs' phase rule gives one degree of freedom for the intensive equilibrium conditions of the two phases, but the bulk mixture also requires its phase fraction. This distinguishes the phase-rule count from the two-property state postulate asked here. The source's word "slope" is a typographical substitution for "state".

questions.subtopic: Sublimation of Ice below Triple-Point Pressure
questions.question: Ice, when heated, directly sublimates into water vapour without going through liquid phase when
questions.explanation: For heating ice at a constant pressure below water's triple-point pressure, no stable liquid region is available in the ordinary phase diagram. The solid therefore crosses the solid–vapour equilibrium line and sublimates directly into vapour, so d is correct. A temperature below the triple-point temperature alone is insufficient: the path also depends on pressure, and the negative fusion slope of ordinary ice–water can permit liquid at slightly lower temperatures under elevated pressure. Similarly, being below the much larger critical pressure does not force sublimation. The source's final sentence is too broad: lowering pressure does not invariably create vapour at every temperature, and lowering temperature below the triple-point value does not invariably create solid at every pressure. The low-pressure heating condition in the question is the relevant criterion.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.question: When a material solidify due to latent heat of fusion is known as:
questions.explanation: The intended phenomenon is thermal arrest, d: during solidification of a pure material at fixed pressure, latent heat is released as liquid becomes solid, producing a constant-temperature plateau or arrest in its cooling curve while the phase change proceeds. The term refers to that arrest, rather than to the entire cooling curve. Thermometry is the measurement of temperature. The source's last bullet is incorrect: subcooling describes a liquid temperature below its saturation/boiling temperature at the specified pressure; in solidification, supercooling or undercooling means a liquid remains liquid below its equilibrium freezing temperature until nucleation occurs. These processes lower the actual liquid temperature relative to the relevant phase-change temperature, rather than lowering the boiling point itself.

questions.subtopic: Specific-Heat Ratio from R and C_v
questions.question: If the value of a gas constant is 0.1 kJ/kg.K and specific heat at constant volume is 0.2 kJ/kg.K, the specific heat ratio will be:
questions.explanation:
For an ideal gas C_p − C_v = R. Substituting C_v = 0.2 kJ/(kg·K) and R = 0.1 kJ/(kg·K) gives C_p = C_v + R = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3 kJ/(kg·K). The specific-heat ratio is dimensionless:
γ = C_p/C_v = 0.3/0.2 = 1.5.
Therefore a is correct. The source's continuation at the top of the next column supplies the same ratio and final value.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.subtopic: Vanishing Latent Heat at the Critical Point
questions.question: At critical pressure
questions.explanation: At the critical saturation state, reached at the critical pressure and its corresponding critical temperature, the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour states become identical. Thus h_fg = h_g − h_f tends to zero, giving b. The T–s diagram illustrates the finite phase-change entropy interval below the critical point; at criticality that interval closes, and h_fg = T(s_g − s_f) vanishes. Entropy itself is not thereby zero, and a real fluid at criticality does not obey the ideal-gas law. The pressure wording is understood along the saturation curve: merely setting p = p_c at an arbitrary temperature is not a specification of the critical state.

questions.subtopic: Limits of Ideal-Gas Behaviour for Vapours
questions.question: Gas laws are least valid in the cases of
questions.explanation: The intended comparison concerns the ideal-gas laws. Vapours near saturation are often relatively dense and close to condensation, so intermolecular attractions and finite molecular volume make pV = mRT a poor approximation; c is the conventional answer. Monatomic, polyatomic and mixed gases can all approach ideal behaviour at sufficiently low density. This is a regime-dependent comparison: a dilute, highly superheated vapour can also behave approximately ideally, while any gas can depart strongly from the ideal-gas law at sufficiently high pressure or near its critical state.

questions.subtopic: Adiabatic Mixing Temperature of Water Streams
questions.question: In a shower mixer, cold water at 27 deg C, flowing at 5 kg/min is mixed with hot water at 77 deg C flowing at 15 kg/min. The exit temperature of the mixture is
questions.explanation:
For steady adiabatic mixing with no shaft work and negligible kinetic/potential changes, the inlet and outlet enthalpy flow rates balance. Taking liquid-water specific heat C_pw as the same constant for both streams,
ṁ_c C_pw T_c + ṁ_h C_pw T_h = (ṁ_c + ṁ_h)C_pw T_out.
Thus (5 × C_pw × 27) + (15 × C_pw × 77) = (5 + 15)C_pw T_out. Cancelling C_pw gives T_out = (5 × 27 + 15 × 77)/20 = (135 + 1155)/20 = 64.5°C, so b is correct. Using Celsius is valid here because the temperature-reference offset cancels through mass conservation.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.subtopic: Maximum Coexisting Phases of One Component
questions.question: In a single component system, the maximum number of phases that can coexist together in equilibrium is _____.
questions.explanation: For an ordinary nonreacting equilibrium system with only pressure and temperature as external variables, Gibbs' phase rule is F = C − P + 2. With one component, C = 1, so F = 3 − P. The number of independent equilibrium degrees of freedom cannot be negative; hence P ≤ 3. The maximum is therefore three phases, c, occurring at a triple point where F = 0. This reproduces the complete printed conclusion: a single component can have three coexisting phases at a triple point and its equilibrium pressure and temperature are then fixed.

(P + a/V²)(V) = RT
[According to Vanderwall's equation]
(P + a/V²)V = Constant ⇒
(P₁ + a/V₁²)V₁ = (P₂ + a/V₂²)V₂
⇒ (10 + a/1²)1 = (P₂ + a/2²)2
⇒ (10 + a)/2 = P₂ + a/4
⇒ 5 + a/2 = P₂ + a/4
⇒ 5 + a/4 = P₂ and a > 0 is given
∴ The value of P₂ should be slightly greater than 5 bar.

questions.subtopic: Ideal Turbine Expansion on a Mollier Chart
questions.question: On Mollier chart a flow though a turbine is represented by:
questions.explanation: A Mollier chart plots specific enthalpy h vertically against specific entropy s horizontally. In the ideal reversible adiabatic turbine model, the expansion is isentropic: s₂ = s₁. Its path therefore runs vertically downward as enthalpy decreases, giving b under the model intended by the source. With negligible kinetic/potential changes the ideal specific turbine work is w_t = h₁ − h₂. A real adiabatic turbine generates entropy, so s₂ > s₁ and its expansion is not a vertical isentropic line. The source's assertion must therefore be restricted to an ideal isentropic turbine; turbine flow in general does not have the single shape stated.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.question: Which of the following options can always be approximated to be an ideal gas?
questions.explanation: The ideal-gas approximation neglects intermolecular forces and the volume occupied by molecules compared with the container volume. A highly superheated, sufficiently dilute vapour is therefore the intended choice (a); saturated vapour and a dense supercritical fluid are not generally ideal. Water vapour mixed with air is commonly treated as ideal when its partial pressure is sufficiently low. Steam means water in its vapour phase; it need not be at an exceptionally high temperature, and it can be approximated as ideal when the state permits. The word “always” in the question is too strong: superheat by itself does not guarantee negligible real-gas effects at arbitrary pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following law governs the isothermal process
questions.explanation:
Boyle’s law governs an isothermal process for a fixed mass of ideal gas: T = constant and P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ = constant.
For comparison, Charles’s law applies at constant pressure, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ = constant. Gay-Lussac’s law applies at constant volume: pressure varies directly with absolute temperature, so P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ = constant.
Therefore (a) is correct.

The critical point is the endpoint where the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour lines meet and the phase distinction disappears. For a specified pure substance its critical temperature and pressure are fixed; if the state is constrained to remain exactly critical, there is no adjustable intensive variable, giving the intended answer F = 0, (c). This is a special critical-point constraint and is not obtained by treating liquid and vapour as two distinct phases in the ordinary phase rule.
For water, T_c ≈ 374°C and modern P_c ≈ 220.64 bar; the source prints 221.2 bar. The latent heat of vaporization goes to zero at the critical point. Along the ordinary liquid–vapour saturation curve, raising pressure raises the boiling temperature and the latent heat tends to decrease to zero at criticality.
The source’s region table reads: critical point—0 degrees of freedom; subcooled region—2; wet region—1; superheated region—2. In the single-phase regions two independent intensive properties specify the state; along saturation pressure and temperature are dependent. For a two-phase mixture an additional quality is required for total mixture properties.

questions.question: Consider the following statements for a throttling process. 1. It is an adiabatic process 2. There is no work transfer in the process 3. Entropy increases in throttling process Which of these statements are correct?
questions.explanation: An ordinary throttling device is modeled as a steady adiabatic flow with no shaft work. Neglecting kinetic and potential energy changes, the steady-flow energy equation then gives h₁ = h₂. A finite pressure drop through the restriction is irreversible; with Q = 0 the entropy balance gives s₂ − s₁ = s_gen > 0. Thus all three statements are correct, (a). questions.explanation: At the same saturation pressure, vaporization and condensation connect the same saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour states in opposite directions. questions.explanation: For an ideal-gas mixture at common temperature and pressure, volume fraction equals mole fraction y_i. questions.question: Under thermal equilibrium, flow of steam is
questions.explanation: Thermal equilibrium means there is no net heat transfer caused by a temperature difference. It does not, by itself, determine the entropy change of a flowing steam stream. Isentropic flow additionally requires the relevant adiabatic and internally reversible idealization; friction, mixing and finite pressure losses can generate entropy even when a flow is insulated or thermally balanced. Thus the source’s asserted isentropic answer (a) does not follow from the stem, and none of the listed process labels is guaranteed.

questions.topic: Properties of Pure Substances, Gases and Gas Mixture
questions.question: For real gases Cp = Cy at :
questions.explanation: Heat capacity depends on the material, its amount and its state. For approximately constant molar heat capacity C, the source writes Q = nCΔT, where Q is heat input, n is amount in moles and ΔT is temperature rise. At constant pressure heat input changes enthalpy and defines Cₚ; at constant volume it changes internal energy and defines Cᵥ. In a stable single phase, Cₚ − Cᵥ = T V α²/κ_T ≥ 0. In the regular third-law low-temperature limit both heat capacities tend to zero and their difference vanishes, which is the formal reason behind source choice (c), absolute zero. A real substance will not remain an ordinary equilibrium gas down to absolute zero, and cₚ > cᵥ is not an unrestricted statement at every limiting state.

questions.sourceExplanation:
Heat capacity depends on nature, size and composition of the substance in the system.
The heat-capacity equation is Q = nCΔT. Q is heat supplied; n is number of moles; C is molar heat capacity; ΔT is temperature change.
Cₚ is heat capacity at constant pressure: heat absorbed or released by unit mass with change in temperature at constant pressure. The temperature change changes the enthalpy of the system.
Cᵥ is heat capacity at constant volume: heat absorbed or released by unit mass at constant volume.
The value of Cₚ is always greater than Cᵥ. But at absolute zero temperature Cₚ = Cᵥ.

questions.question:
The critical point and triple point data for water are T_c = 374°C, P_c = 22.1 MPa, T_T = 0.01°C, P_T = 0.6 kPa. Indicate the phase change that will occur in the following cases:
(i) Ice at 0.5 kPa is heated isobarically.
(ii) Water vapour at 400°C is compressed isothermally.
Use the labeled P–T diagram.
questions.explanation:
(i) The stated pressure 0.5 kPa is below the triple-point pressure, about 0.6 kPa. Isobaric heating is a horizontal path on the P–T diagram, AB, and crosses the solid–vapour boundary: ice sublimates without a stable liquid stage.
(ii) At 400°C the temperature exceeds water’s critical temperature near 374°C. Isothermal compression is a vertical path, CD, and does not cross a liquid–vapour phase boundary; a distinct liquid cannot be formed by pressure alone above T_c.
Therefore the diagram paths are (i) AB and (ii) CD, option (a). The source explanation repeats the critical pressure as 22.1 kPa; the question correctly gives 22.1 MPa. Its explanation also says 370°C although the specified temperature is 400°C.

questions.question: The magnitude of which one of the following quantity does not indicate the departure of a real gas from the ideal gas behavior:
questions.explanation: Compressibility factor Z differs from 1 for a nonideal gas, and a nonzero Joule–Kelvin coefficient indicates real-gas throttling behaviour. Fugacity f is an effective pressure: ideal gases have f = P, so the fugacity coefficient f/P or departure of f from P measures nonideality. Entropy itself has no universal ideal-gas benchmark and its absolute magnitude does not by itself measure departure from ideal-gas behaviour. The standard checked answer is therefore (d), rather than the source’s (c).

questions.question: A pressure-cooker contains water at 100°C with liquid volume being one-tenth of vapour volume. At 100°C, the specific volume for saturated liquid and saturated vapour are 0.001 m³/kg and 1.6 m³/kg, respectively. The dryness fraction for the mixture is
questions.explanation:
Let total volume be V. The liquid volume is one tenth of vapour volume: V_f = V_g/10, so V_g = 10V/11 and V_f = V/11. With v_g = 1.6 m³/kg and v_f = 0.001 m³/kg,
m_g = (10V/11)/1.6,
m_f = (V/11)/0.001.
Quality x = m_g/(m_f + m_g) = (10/1.6)/[(10/1.6) + 1000] = 6.25/1006.25 = 1/161 ≈ 0.006211.
Thus (b); a large vapour volume can still contain little vapour mass because of its much lower density.

questions.question: The equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT is known as
questions.explanation: The equation (P + a/v²)(v − b) = RT is the van der Waals equation of state, choice (d). The ideal-gas model treats molecules as point particles with elastic collisions and negligible interactions, a good approximation for dilute gases. Van der Waals’s modification, proposed in 1873, accounts for finite molecular size through excluded volume b and intermolecular attractions through a/v². These effects can produce measurable departures from ideal-gas behaviour.

Van der Waals equation: (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT.
The ideal gas law treats gas molecules as point particles with perfectly elastic collisions. This works well for dilute gases in many experimental circumstances. But gas molecules are not point masses, and their properties can have an experimentally measurable effect. Johannes D. van der Waals proposed a modification in 1873 to take into account molecular size and molecular interaction forces. It is usually referred to as the van der Waals equation of state.

questions.question: The pressure p of an ideal gas and its mean kinetic energy E per unit volume are related by the relation
questions.explanation:
For an ideal gas, c_rms = √(3RᵤT/M), where M is molar mass. The mass of one molecule is m₀ = M/N_A, so its mean translational kinetic energy is
ε̄ = ½m₀c_rms² = ½(M/N_A)(3RᵤT/M) = 3RᵤT/(2N_A).
From PV = nRᵤT, RᵤT = PV/n. Hence ε̄ = 3PV/(2nN_A). Since nN_A is the number of molecules, the kinetic energy per volume is E = ε̄(nN_A)/V = 3P/2. Therefore P = 2E/3, choice (d).

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
1. Availability is the maximum theoretical work obtainable.
2. Clapeyron’s equation for dry saturated steam is given by (v_s − v_f) = (dT_s/dP)[(h_s − h_f)/T_s].
3. A gas can have any temperature at a given pressure unlike a vapour, which has a fixed temperature at a given pressure.
4. Joule–Thomson coefficient is expressed as μ = (∂s/∂P)ₕ.
Of these statements:
questions.explanation: Statement 1 gives the usual meaning of availability: maximum useful work as a system comes into equilibrium with its specified surroundings. Statement 2 is the rearranged Clapeyron relation, v_s − v_f = (dT_s/dP)(h_s − h_f)/T_s, and is correct. Statement 4 is false: the Joule–Thomson coefficient is (∂T/∂P)ₕ, not the printed (∂s/∂P)ₕ. Statement 3 is true only if “vapour” means saturated vapour in liquid–vapour equilibrium. A superheated vapour can have different temperatures at one pressure, so the unrestricted printed statement is false. With that literal reading only 1 and 2 are correct, and no printed option matches. Source (a) assumes the saturated-vapour interpretation.

questions.question: Which one is not a Maxwell equation
questions.explanation:
The first three printed choices are valid Maxwell relations:
(∂V/∂S)ₚ = (∂T/∂p)ₛ,
(∂V/∂T)ₚ = −(∂S/∂p)ₜ,
(∂T/∂V)ₛ = −(∂p/∂S)ᵥ.
The fourth is printed with constant-pressure subscript on (∂P/∂T)ₚ, which would be zero and is not the Maxwell relation. The correct fourth relation is (∂P/∂T)ᵥ = (∂S/∂V)ₜ. Thus (d) is not a Maxwell equation.

questions.question: Which equation of state for a gas is an improvement of the ideal gas law?
questions.explanation:
The source intends van der Waals’s equation, (P + n²a/V²)(V − nb) = nRᵤT, which improves on the ideal-gas model by allowing molecular excluded volume and intermolecular attraction. Here P is pressure, n amount in moles, V total volume, T absolute temperature, a and b substance constants, and Rᵤ = 8.3145 J/(mol·K) when pressure and volume use consistent SI units. The source labels pressure in atm while giving R in joules; those units require conversion.
However, the Beattie–Bridgeman equation in (a) and the Clausius real-gas equation in (c) are also equations of state developed to improve ideal-gas behaviour. The unrestricted stem therefore does not uniquely identify (d).

questions.question: A car tube contains air at 200 kPa pressure in the cold night of temperature (—10°C). During the day time, the volume of the tube is found to be increased by 9.5%. Find out day temperature and change in pressure.
questions.explanation:
For a fixed amount of ideal gas, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. The data give P₁ = 200 kPa, T₁ ≈ 263 K and V₂ = 1.095V₁, so
P₂ = (200/1.095)(T₂/263).
This is one equation for the two unknowns P₂ and T₂; an additional condition is required. The source’s proposed pair 15°C and 219 kPa does not satisfy it: 15°C is 288 K, and then P₂ ≈ 200 kPa. If P₂ = 219 kPa, the required T₂ ≈ 315.3 K ≈ 42.2°C. The source also incorrectly writes 298 K = 15°C. No displayed numerical pair is supported, and “change in pressure” is not the final pressure itself.

questions.question: Clapeyron equation represents the dependence of
questions.explanation:
The Maxwell relation (∂P/∂T)ᵥ = (∂s/∂v)ₜ applied across equilibrium liquid–vapour coexistence gives
dP_sat/dT = (s_g − s_f)/(v_g − v_f) = s_fg/v_fg.
Because s_fg = h_fg/T,
dP_sat/dT = h_fg/[T(v_g − v_f)].
This is the Clapeyron relation: it describes the dependence of saturation pressure on saturation temperature, so (b) is the most precise choice. It also links specific volume and enthalpy changes across the boundary. During a phase change at one specified saturation state, pressure and temperature stay fixed as quality and total volume change; along the saturation curve P and T vary together.

questions.sourceExplanation:
According to Maxwell’s third relationship, (∂P/∂T)ᵥ = (∂S/∂V)ₜ. When saturated liquid converts to saturated vapour at constant temperature and pressure, during evaporation pressure and temperature are independent of volume.
(dP/dT)_sat = (S_g − S_f)/(V_g − V_f) = S_fg/V_fg.
But S_g − S_f = h_fg/T.
(dP/dT)_sat = h_fg/[T(V_g − V_f)].
This is Clausius–Clapeyron equation, representing dependence of saturation pressure on saturation temperature. Clapeyron equation relates temperature, specific volume, pressure and enthalpy.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer:
List-I
A. Bottle filling of gas
B. Nernst–Simon statement
C. Joule–Thomson effect
D. ∫p dv

List-II
1. Absolute zero temperature
2. Variable flow
3. Quasi-static path

questions.explanation: A. Bottle filling of gas → 2. Variable flow, since mass in the bottle changes with time. B. Nernst–Simon statement → 1. Absolute zero temperature. C. Joule–Thomson effect → 4. questions.question:
For a perfect gas match List I with List II:
List I
A. Isobaric thermal expansion coefficient
B. Isothermal compressibility
C. Isentropic compressibility
D. Joule–Thomson coefficient

List II
1. 0
2. ∞
3. 1/v
4. 1/T
5. 1/p
6. 1/(γp)
questions.explanation:
For a perfect gas, pv = RT.
A. Isobaric expansion coefficient α = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)ₚ = 1/T → 4.
B. Isothermal compressibility κ_T = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)ₜ = 1/p → 5.
C. Isentropic compressibility κ_s = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)ₛ = 1/(γp), from pv^γ = constant → 6.
D. Joule–Thomson coefficient μ = (∂T/∂p)ₕ = 0 → 1.
Therefore A–4, B–5, C–6, D–1, choice (c).

questions.question: The maximum work, that can be obtained from a system during a given process in which the initial and final temperatures of the system are equal to the surrounding temperature, is equal to the decrease in :
questions.explanation: For a closed system exchanging heat with a reservoir at fixed surrounding temperature T₀, the first law gives W = Q − ΔU. The entropy inequality gives Q ≤ T₀ΔS, so W ≤ T₀ΔS − ΔU. If both endpoint temperatures equal T₀, F = U − T₀S at the endpoints and the reversible maximum total work is W_max = −ΔF. Hence (b). This is total work under the thermal-reservoir assumptions; any required displacement of an external constant-pressure atmosphere must be accounted for when defining useful work. Gibbs free energy G = H − TS supplies the familiar non-expansion-work potential when temperature and pressure are fixed.

questions.question: The expression indicating Y as a thermodynamic property is:
questions.explanation:
A thermodynamic property has an exact differential. Interpreting the printed expression for Y as its differential form, option (a) is
dY = XZ dZ + ½Z² dX = d(½XZ²).
The mixed derivatives agree: ∂(XZ)/∂X = Z and ∂(½Z²)/∂Z = Z. The other displayed forms do not satisfy this exactness criterion for independent variables. Thus (a). The source writes Y = rather than dY =, a notational omission retained in the printed choices.

questions.question: The state of a real gas is changed from pressure P₁, temperature T₁ to pressure P₂, temperature T₂. The change in enthalpy h₂ − h₁ is given by
questions.explanation:
For a real simple compressible substance, dh = T ds + v dP. Express entropy in T and P:
ds = (cₚ/T)dT − (∂v/∂T)ₚdP.
Substitution gives dh = cₚdT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)ₚ]dP. Integrating along a suitable two-step path between the states gives the form in (d): a temperature integral of cₚ and a pressure integral of the bracket. For example, evaluate the first integral at P₁, then the second at T₂.
The printed choice (c) and source explanation incorrectly use cᵥ and a derivative with respect to pressure while holding pressure constant. The correct choice is (d), which has cₚ and the constant-pressure temperature derivative.

questions.question: The Joule-Thomson effect is not exhibited by
questions.explanation:
The Joule–Thomson coefficient describes the temperature response to an isenthalpic pressure change:
μ = (∂T/∂P)ₕ = [T(∂v/∂T)ₚ − v]/cₚ.
For an ideal gas v = RT/P, so T(∂v/∂T)ₚ − v = T(R/P) − RT/P = 0. Thus ideal gases show no Joule–Thomson temperature change, choice (a). Positive μ denotes cooling on a pressure drop, negative μ denotes heating, and μ = 0 on an inversion curve.

questions.question: For a refrigerant being used in a vapour compression refrigeration system, the Joule- Thomson coefficient should be
questions.explanation: A conventional vapour-compression refrigerator uses a throttling valve to reduce refrigerant pressure and temperature before the evaporator. Since dT = μ_JT dP and dP < 0, cooling through that pressure reduction requires μ_JT > 0, choice (a). The source selects negative μ by confusing the refrigerant’s subsequent absorption of heat in the evaporator with its temperature change through the adiabatic valve. Its own sign table states μ > 0 → cooling and μ < 0 → heating; the correct coefficient for the intended throttling cooling is positive.

questions.question: When a real gas follows Joule Thomson expansion process, the temperature
questions.explanation: For a real gas, μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)ₕ depends on state, so an isenthalpic pressure drop can cool or heat the gas, choice (d). In terms of expansion coefficient α, μ_JT = v(Tα − 1)/cₚ. It is zero at an inversion point; the locus of those points is the inversion curve. Positive μ produces cooling and negative μ heating because dP < 0. Many gases cool in their ordinary operating range, while hydrogen at room temperature warms because its inversion temperature is low. For an ideal gas μ = 0 and throttling produces no temperature change; a nonzero coefficient therefore indicates nonideal behaviour.

questions.sourceExplanation:
When a real gas follows Joule–Thomson expansion, temperature may increase or decrease.
The Joule–Thomson coefficient μ is the ratio of temperature change to pressure drop and is expressed in terms of thermal expansion coefficient. It is zero at a point called inversion point for real gases. Expansion of most real gases causes cooling when the coefficient is positive and gas temperature is below inversion temperature. At atmospheric pressure hydrogen has low inversion temperature and warms during Joule–Thomson expansion at room temperature. Since ideal-gas throttling has no temperature change, a nonzero coefficient refers to a real gas.

questions.question: For achieving the cooling effect by Joule- Kelvin, expansion the initial temperature of gas must be below the
questions.explanation: Joule–Kelvin expansion is throttling. Cooling requires positive μ_JT in the initial state. A necessary temperature condition is that the gas begin below its maximum inversion temperature, choice (c); above that maximum it cannot lie in the cooling region at any pressure. Being below the maximum alone is not sufficient at every pressure—the state must lie on the cooling side of the inversion curve.

questions.explanation: The Joule–Thomson process is throttling through a porous plug, valve or other restriction, choice (a). questions.question: The change in specific volume during vaporization of a refrigerant is 0.035 m³/kg. The slope of the saturation curve on a pressure–temperature diagram at 20°C is 17.69 kPa/K. The enthalpy of vaporization of the refrigerant is:
questions.explanation:
By the Clapeyron equation, dP_sat/dT = h_fg/[T(v_g − v_f)]. Thus
h_fg = (dP_sat/dT)TΔv
= 17.69 kPa/K × (273 + 20) K × 0.035 m³/kg
= 181.408 kJ/kg ≈ 181.5 kJ/kg.
Using 293.15 K gives 181.501 kJ/kg. Since 1 kPa·m³ = 1 kJ, the dimensions are correct and choice (b) follows.
